title: Error-Adaptive Quasi-local Decoding of the Toric Code
authors: Hossein Dehghani, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Michael Gullans
abstract: Topological quantum memories need decoders that are both reliable and scalable, but these goals compete: globally informed decoders are accurate near threshold yet expensive, while strictly local rules are fast but can miss long-range structure. Motivated by recent recoverability and mixed-state viewpoints, we make this tradeoff operational for the dephased toric code through a decoder-level local recoverability diagnostic. We compare global MWPM corrections to quasi-local corrections inside a target region and define a matching ratio $R_{\mathrm{match}}$, with mismatch $ε_{\mathrm{match}}=1-R_{\mathrm{match}}$. Across geometry families, $ε_{\mathrm{match}}$ shows strong buffer-controlled suppression and is well organized by a two-geometry scaling form. For scaled families, especially $a=b=d/8$, $R_{\mathrm{match}}$ exhibits a clear crossing and finite-size collapse near $p\!\sim\!0.09$, consistent with a growing recoverability scale near the decoding transition. We use this scaling to formulate an adaptive buffer-selection rule and to identify a distance-scaled initialization for a composite quasi-local RG decoder on the full torus. In the tuned family $a_0=b_0=d/8$, the resulting logical-failure curves show an apparent finite-size crossing at $p\simeq0.09$--$0.10$, below the conventional MWPM threshold scale. We focus on dephasing noise with perfect syndrome measurements to cleanly isolate the underlying behavior.
summary: This paper tackles the scalability challenge in topological quantum error correction by introducing a 'matching ratio' diagnostic to quantify local recoverability. This diagnostic is used to build a composite, quasi-local Renormalization Group decoder for the Toric Code. The resulting decoder exhibits threshold behavior, suggesting a viable path toward fault-tolerant quantum computation that balances accuracy and computational cost.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental trade-off in topological quantum error correction between achieving global accuracy near the threshold and maintaining the computational locality required for scalable, practical decoders.
main_result: By developing an adaptive, composite quasi-local decoder based on a matching ratio diagnostic, the authors demonstrate a threshold-like logical-failure behavior that appears at a lower error rate than conventional global decoders.
method: The core method involves defining a 'matching ratio' ($R_{	ext{match}}$) comparing local decoding results to global ones, which is then used to formulate an adaptive, multi-scale Renormalization Group (RG) decoder structure.
model_or_system: The study analyzes the dephased Toric Code, which is a model for topological quantum memory, using syndrome measurements under dephasing noise.
key_observables: Matching ratio ($R_{	ext{match}}$), mismatch ($\epsilon_{	ext{match}}$), and the logical-failure curve crossing point ($p_{	ext{comp}} 	imes$).
important_parameters: Error rate ($p$), target region size ($a$), buffer width ($b$), and code distance ($d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses specifically on dephasing noise with perfect syndrome measurements, and the matching ratio uses literal Pauli-string equality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the local/buffer regions, show the scaling collapse of $R_{	ext{match}}$ for specific geometries, and display the final logical-failure curves for the composite decoder.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the local-global trade-off, develops the matching ratio diagnostic, uses this to derive scaling laws, and finally implements and analyzes a composite, quasi-local RG decoder structure.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, theoretically motivated, and computationally structured approach to designing fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols by bridging the gap between idealized global theory and practical local computation.

The local decoder acts on a target square A of linear size a (blue) to- gether with a surrounding buffer region B of width b (red). The full system is a distance-d toric code with periodic bound- ary conditions (not shown), drawn on the underlying 2d × 2d grid; one X-stabilizer (vertex) lattice spacing corresponds to two grid units, and a and b are quoted in vertex-lattice spac- ings throughout the paper.

FIG. 2. Numerical scaling of the local-global mismatch. (a) ln ϵmatch versus ln a. (b) ln ϵmatch for the constrained family a = b. (c) ln ϵmatch versus b. Panel (a) isolates target-size dependence, panel (b) probes the scaled family used later in the decoder construction, and panel (c) isolates buffer-size dependence. Taken together, the three panels motivate the two-geometry ansatz in Eq. (6) rather than a single-variable CMI-style scaling form controlled only by buffer width. All panels are at d = 64, with the complementary length held fixed at vertex scale 4 (b = 4 in (a), a = 4 in (c)); error bars are 1σ statistical. Black lines are fits to Eq. FIG. 3. Crossing and finite-size scaling of the matching ratio for the scaled family a = b = d/8. (a) Crossing behavior of Rmatch(p) across code distances. (b) Corresponding finite-size collapse around p0. The crossing signals transition-like behavior of the local-global agreement once the local support is scaled with system size.

FIG. 4. Error-adaptive choice of the buffer size. (a) Rmatch versus b for representative physical error rates p; the dashed line marks the agreement level Rmatch = 1−η = 0.98 corresponding to η = 0.02. (b) Adaptive buffer size bc(p, η) extracted from the same fixed-geometry data, shown for target mismatch tolerances η = 0.01–0.05; the required buffer grows as p approaches the transition and as the tolerance η is tightened. This analysis motivates the distance-scaled initialization used for the composite decoder below.

FIG. 5. Composite quasi-local decoder architecture. (a) Adjacent local regions Ai with overlapping buffers Bi at RG round r, and their merge to a larger region at RG round (r+1). Local sectors with no residual defects or with two bulk defects are resolved within RG round r, while boundary-associated residual defects are paired after the merge step. Blue segments mark the defect-pairing paths used to annihilate syndrome defects and correct errors. (b) Two-step checkerboard schedule used to parallelize patch updates without double counting on neighboring regions.
